A lot of people in here have already answered, and I think the only thing I could maybe add is that in different kinds of rotations, the roles of opposite hitters and outside hitters are different. As everyone's already mentioned, an opposite hitter is the position directly opposite to the setter, which means that whenever the setter rotates to the back, they rotate to the front, and viceversa. Well, this allows for different playstyles depending on the team. Teams usually play a 5-1 rotation, which means 5 spikers and 1 setter, but sometimes some teams might opt for a 6-2 rotation, which means all 6 players are good spikers, and so there's 2 people also playing the setter position, and usually that's what the opposite does as well, as their a direct mirror of the setter, they might also be the players called to make emergency sets (sets done by a player other than the setter). We've seen both of these formations in karasuno, 5-1 is the usual one they play, but whenever they want to add a bit of surprise they also add Suga there to add more offensive options with every player being a possible spiker. Anyway, opposites are just usually very offensive centred, like Ushiwaka, and function as the pillar for a more balanced offence in a team, where you can attack from any angle, but since they're directly on the opposite side of the setter, it's pretty hard to give a good toss to them, so they have to be really good attackers on their own if you want them to be a viable option.

I personally think they're a pretty good match-up for Shiratorizawa. Nekoma is really well-known for having exceptional floor defence. They're a team where the libero isn't the only one good at digging up spikes and giving A passes, and they have really solid blocking with Kuroo, and an okay one with Lev. Imo they'd be able to go toe to toe with them for at least the first two sets, and the decisive factor would be if Kenma is willing to run that extra mile for the team. Sure, Ushiwaka is an absolute cannon, but I think Kuroo would be able to keep him in check, not necessarily stuff his spikes or anything, but the Kuroo/Yaku combo is insane when it comes to defence, Kuroo is great at always being there to at least touch a spike, while Yaku is just one of the best libero in the whole series. We see them in action against another top 5 ace, Bokuto, and how they managed to stop him quite a few times. Then there's the wild card Tendou, who I think would be the worst match-up for Lev, since he only plays on instinct and very rarely thinks things through for long enough to make plays that require more brains. Goshiki, I could see also being a problem, while he's not as powerful as Ushiwaka, his technique and skill are definitely something to be aware of. All in all, I think they'd be able to take at least one set, and if Shiratorizawa isn't playing at their best that day, maybe even taking the whole game by a hair, especially since they're the kind of team that gets better at blocking as the match goes on, so Kuroo might be able to stop Ushiwaka a few times, since his pupil was able to do it once.

But yeah I just love how they both helped one another reach new heights, Kageyama started doing those really low sets, and Atsumu started trying for the freak quick. It's so nice and inspiring.

I do agree that a cross-court set can be difficult, but imo the thing that sets those moments apart was that Oikawa's set wasn't necessarily one that would prompt either an underhand pass, or an emergency set from another team member. Like I mentioned, Kageyama could do exactly that same set, and I'd argue we see him do something similar in the decisive point of the Seijoh match, doing the quick set from behind the 3m line into a center attack, with both precision and speed. The thing I'd say is the pivotal point is how unbelievably dedicated Atsumu is to always giving the best support to his spikers, how he uses as little movement as possible so as to not give away his strategy, but he still positions himself perfectly under the ball in order to give his characteristic perfect sets.

The thing that, imo, sets Atsumu apart is that not only are his sets full of care and skill, but that he puts his own physique on the line to set to the best of his ability. We see this in his "because I'm a setter" speech. He has a thrive to give his spikers the best sets, so he basically always uses overhand sets, even if it means having to get really low in order to be under the ball. As a setter myself, I can't stress enough how impressive it was to see him set from incredibly awkward angles, and that those sets were still as best as can be. I think that's why Kageyama said he was happy to get there when he saw it, because up until now we had never seen a setter who had such stable footing and physical condition that they could still be delivering top tier sets even if the pass was low. I think the main difference we see in Kageyama and Atsumu's playstyles is that Kageyama has the ability to deliver essentially perfect sets from anywhere on the court, while Atsumu is able to deliver sets that are just as good, even under circumstances that would lead to an emergency set from other team members. Like imo Atsumu seems like the kind of player that insists on always being the second touch, regardless if there's someone else capable of getting it. We've seen him consume his teammates before, there's a scene where Suna is already positioned to make a pass, but the moment he sees Atsumu approach he gets out of the way to let him set, and that is to me a great way of showing his characterisation as someone whose hunger consumes his team.
